subject: calderMobile
pitch:
Category: Abstract.
Subject: hanging mobile.
Style: Alexander Calder.
reasoning:
I'm thinking this should be an abstract Calder-style hanging mobile rather than a creature, so the pieces can be simple shapes without joints. Since it hangs from above, I'm considering whether the lowest point should rest near floor level, keeping the elevated placement the pitch describes, similar to how a hanging lantern retains its height off the ground.

I'll add a small ceiling disc at the top around y=1.9, then design a Calder-style mobile with hierarchical balanced arms holding flat organic shapes in black, red, yellow, blue, and white. I'm planning a recursive tree structure for the arms with wire pivots and hinge joints, computing torque balance so each arm hangs level, and sketching a function to build each node recursively from a parent joint.

Defining the arm and item types...

I'm figuring out the hierarchical positioning: shapes hang from a top loop, arms pivot at their attachment point with ends extending outward by length and split ratio, and children recursively hang downward from those end points by their drop distance.

For balance, I want each arm's two sides to be weighted by the total mass of whatever's attached, so heavier branches get shorter arm segments—computing weight recursively as shape area or summed child weights, then deriving the split ratio from that. I'll clamp the split so very lopsided weights don't collapse one side to nothing, accepting a slight balance compromise for visual stability.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: each arm gets a pivot joint chained from its parent's end point, and each shape gets its own hinge joint so it can spin freely, totaling roughly 22 joints across the mobile. I'm working out how the wires/rods connect each pivot down to its child, tying bone assignments to the correct parent joints.

For the shapes, I'm thinking of each as a flat painted plate extruded in a plane, with orientation defined by an x-direction and y-direction—mostly keeping y vertical for hanging plates with some yaw rotation, but letting some plates lie flat horizontally like discs with thickness along x instead.

I'm working out a helper function to define plate orientation combining yaw and tilt, computing a horizontal direction and perpendicular vector so the plate can hang at an angle from a hook rather than perfectly flat. Each outline is centered at the origin with a hook point at the top, so the attachment point is offset from the shape's center along its local up direction.

Now I'm sketching out a shape library — discs, leaves, crescents, teardrops, stars, fish tails, ovals — each defined as unit-coordinate point sets that get scaled, with varying smoothing applied for Calder-style organic or sharp mobile pieces.

For the shapes, I'm generating polar blobs via a radius function sampled around the circle, keeping it simple with 24 segments and no smoothing for cleaner polygonal mobile pieces. At the top of each shape I'm adding a tiny wire loop (a small torus oriented in the plate's plane) to act as the hanging eyelet, with the connecting wire running down into the plate.

For the crescent moon shape, I'm computing the outer arc and an offset inner arc so they meet exactly at the two tips, solving for the inner circle's center and radius so the crescent opening faces right with matching endpoint geometry.

Tracing the outline now: outer arc sweeps from 60° through 180° to 300° for the outer tip, then the inner arc runs back from 289.1° to 70.9° through 180°, forming a closed loop without self-crossing since the inner stays within the outer. The top point (0,1) sits right on the outer arc at 90°, confirming the shape closes cleanly, though I'm noting the crescent hangs a bit lopsided with the opening facing right — I may want to rotate the orientation for better balance.

For figuring out where each shape hangs, I'm thinking about defining a `hook` point for each outline and shifting the whole shape so that hook sits at the origin. For a balanced hang, the hook should align horizontally with the shape's centroid, so I need to approximate the centroid's x-coordinate and then find the topmost outline point at that x-position to use as the hanging point.

I'm thinking about rotating each shape so they open in different directions while still computing balance from centroid, using shoelace for area-based weights. For the paint, I want flat matte Calder-style colors with subtle hand-painted mottling—slightly darker speckled texture with low contrast rather than perfectly flat fills.

I'm considering edge details for the painted sheet metal, and wondering whether to add a small decorative touch like a tiny signature stamp on one plate, though it may be unnecessary and skippable.

Adding decal-like textures too: a spiral disc motif, a dot-on-disc pattern, and a ceiling canopy hook, placing these as thin planes positioned flush against the faces of the shapes using their local coordinate frames.

For the wires, I'm settling on a thin radius with low-poly sides for performance, and planning to give the arms gentle S-curves via Catmull-Rom splines through a few control points, keeping the endpoints fixed but adding slight perpendicular offsets for organic bending.

Orienting the torus axis horizontally perpendicular to the arm direction using an aim/up configuration. I'm reconsidering the arm shape too—rather than a sine sag, I'll keep rods mostly straight but curve the last stretch upward near the end using a small catmull curve.

I'll make the S-curve offset opposite-signed on each side of the pivot so it's zero at both endpoints and the joint, sampling nine points for the catmull path, and explicitly assign the bone to the nearest joint for rigid skinning. Now I'm moving on to planning the top-down layout.

For the overall structure, I'll set the ceiling canopy at the top with a wire down to the first arm, defining yaws and drop lengths in meters, then solving for heights so the lowest point lands at zero. Since absolute positions depend on cumulative offsets from the top, I'll do this in two passes: first a pure layout pass that computes positions and tracks the minimum y across all shape bounds, then shift everything down so the lowest point touches zero before actually building the geometry.

Each shape's world position comes from its hook point plus axis vectors scaled by its outline coordinates, factoring in yaw and tilt. Now I'm sketching the tree spec itself—canopy wire length, then a main arm branching into secondary arms with their own lengths, yaws, and drops.

Still defining arm structure...

I should figure out shape weights by area based on their radii, keeping arm balance ratios clamped between 0.2 and 0.8. I also need to double check for collisions since shapes hanging from arm ends extend downward and could intersect other arms or pivots if drops are too small relative to shape size.

Checking through the geometry, most shapes seem far enough apart by yaw and horizontal distance to avoid overlap, though I can't fully verify without rendering—I'll accept the layout and move on to computing overall height by tracking each pivot's vertical position.

I'm tallying up the total height down to about 1.95m including the final disc shape, with width around 1.8m—reasonable scale for a large Calder-style mobile. I'll plan to shift everything so the lowest point sits exactly at y=0.

For the hanging mechanism, I'm adding a small ceiling disc with a hook ring at the top, and planning the joint naming structure: a root "mount" joint at the canopy position, plus hinge-role joints for each arm and plate so the rig structure reads clearly.

Working through parent-child relationships for the wires: each wire connects an arm's end hook to a child pivot or shape hook, and since rotation happens around a vertical axis at the child joint, I can attach the wire there without breaking the visual alignment.

For joint orientation I'm defaulting the root to point straight up along +Y when no direction is specified, letting children inherit that vertical bone axis since I'm supplying explicit bone endpoints anyway.

Now I'm working out the extrude parameters—thickness around 6-8mm to mimic Calder's sheet metal plates, deciding to skip bevels to keep triangle count low, and making sure each outline stays simple and star-shaped so it won't self-intersect after rotation and offset.

For the leaf shape, I'm sketching an asymmetric curved outline with sharp tips at top and bottom and smoother bulges along the sides. I realize using built-in smoothing could shift the centroid and top-point calculations slightly, so I decide it's safer to generate dense points myself via a custom smoothing function rather than rely on automatic smoothing.

Writing the corner-cutting logic...

I still need to find a horizontal line hook by computing the polygon centroid and scanning edges for crossings to get the max y, then shift the shape accordingly, plus ensure consistent CCW winding by checking signed area and reversing if needed. I'm also sketching a reusable shape library function that returns point sets and area for different kinds and sizes.

Defining more shape kinds...

Writing the grain and edge-wear logic...

For the textured spiral disc, I'm generating a spiral path overlaid on a white circular plate, applying it as a decal texture on both faces via small offset circle geometries positioned just off the surface in each normal direction.

I'd like to generalize this into a decorate function that handles different patterns per part—spirals, rings, dots, or signature marks—each using transparent-background textures so the base disc color shows through, with stroke colors chosen to contrast (white spiral on black disc, black rings on yellow, etc).

I'm working out how tinting interacts with black/white textures so the multiplication stays correct, then adding a nice extra touch: a thin wire dangling a small black ball from the lowest point of a shape like the red leaf, mimicking Calder's habit of adding small hanging details.

Now I'm designing the pivot collars where arm wires meet—small torus eyelets with a bead at each joint—and setting the wire's thin radius and flat black color for a consistent mobile-arm look.

Now I'm working out the hang point for each child element: the wire ends at the top of its eyelet, and for arm children the pivot sits a short distance below that, with the eyelet ring positioned at the midpoint. I'm treating each shape's origin as this hang point so the plate and eyelet attach consistently.

Defining more layout logic...

I'm working out the vertical placement of the canopy and hanging wires, checking total height against a 2.5m ceiling and realizing it's a bit tall, so I'm shortening the top wire length. I'm tracing through the chain of y-offsets from pivot to arm drops to make sure the hang points stack up correctly.

This seems like a large Calder-style mobile, bigger than a human figure, so I'm fine keeping the total height around 2.3m, maybe trimming the top wire slightly to 2.2. I'm now working out the sizes for each weight shape, like the red leaf and disc elements, scaling them proportionally to the branch lengths.

I'm sketching out the remaining shapes to round out the composition, mixing black, white, and colored forms—discs, crescents, amoebas, ovals, a star—to echo Calder's characteristic palette, and considering swapping one black disc for a white one to balance the color distribution.

Then I'm adding a new branching arm K with a small black disc and a yellow ringed disc dangling off it to extend the structure while keeping the weight distribution reasonable.

Now I'm checking the vertical and lateral placement to make sure K's shapes don't collide with the red leaf hanging off arm B, since their drop distances and arm angles put them fairly close together.

I also want to verify the B and C subtrees stay apart since they hang from opposite ends of A, and that nested elements E, F, G within C don't overlap given their arm angles and drop offsets. I'm now reconsidering A's yaw angle, since 15° points the arm mostly toward the viewer's depth axis rather than across the frame, which would foreshorten it badly from the front-facing camera—so I should increase it toward something like 80° instead.

I'll set plate yaw ranges narrower for front readability, keep most tilts small except a couple steeper ones since these hang freely from a single hook point so orientation is flexible. For connecting elements between joints, I'm defining a rod helper that takes two endpoints, radius, color, and options like bone-color and polygon sides.

Now I'm building the sweep geometry for curved arms using a Catmull-Rom spline with rounded caps, a torus shape for ring elements oriented along a surface normal, spheres for bead details, and a lathe-based canopy profile positioned against the ceiling underside.

I need a root "mount" joint at the canopy hook point, with everything else hanging below it, and a wire connecting the canopy to each arm joint. Now I'm sketching out the import structure for the build script, pulling in the builder utilities, paint, math helpers, and SVG/catmull functions from the SDK, plus the Joint type.

Writing Chaikin smoothing function...

Defining more shape builders...

Writing lacquer paint function...

Toning down the contrast to 7% mixes of black and white for a subtler plate texture. I'm defining a function that builds each shape's joint hierarchy with hinge roles and mobile grouping, then positioning decal textures centered on the shape's centroid using a thin offset plane.

For the textures themselves, I'm drawing a spiral path with rounded strokes across multiple turns, and a rings pattern with concentric circles plus a filled center dot.

For dotsTex, I'm arranging a hex grid of small dots within an elliptical boundary rather than a square one, since the plate is oval-shaped — matching the texture's viewBox aspect ratio to the plane's actual proportions so the dots don't get stretched.

For sigTex, I'm drawing a simple white logo-like mark (an arc plus a triangle) positioned off-center lower on a small decal, tinted white via the part color so it reads clean against the blue surface. I'm placing this decal only on the front face using the surface normal direction, since render order doesn't matter here.

For general decal placement, I'm computing each plane's orientation from the part's local normal and y-axis so front-facing decals draw upright, and back-facing ones (using the inverted normal) still appear correctly oriented rather than mirrored, since the viewer is on the opposite side of the plane. I'm using plain planes with alpha-cutout textures for both artwork and circular marks rather than switching geometry types.

Now I'm working out the thickness axis as the cross product of the plate's x and y axes, then finding the lowest point of the plate's outline in local coordinates so I can attach a dangling wire and ball from that position downward in world space.

I'm now sketching how to build each arm: placing a hinge joint at the pivot point along the arm's length, then defining a sideways offset curve using sine functions split at the pivot fraction so the arm bends naturally on either side, with amplitude scaled relative to the arm's length and direction computed from yaw angle.

Now I'm working out the hook ring geometry at the arm ends, positioning it in the vertical plane perpendicular to the wire direction, then setting up the torus part parameters with bone, direction, and orientation axes.

I'm adding an eyelet ring at the pivot point and a connecting wire from the parent hook through to the pivot, plus a small collar bead sphere to visually cap the joint.

Now I'm working out the wire connections between each element's parent and child joints—for bones connecting to arm joints and for shapes connecting to their own joints—using rod geometry between an offset start point and the target joint. I'm also placing the canopy's eye hook at the top ceiling mount position, feeding a wire down from the canopy to the first arm's pivot.

Setting up the joint hierarchy with the mount joint as the root, defining each part's bone/joint relationships so arm and plate joints reference pivot and hang positions correctly, and marking all joints with a hinge role except the mount.

Now I'm designing the type definitions for shapes and arms, then building the layout structures that compute each shape's hierarchical position, axes, outline points, area, and centroid.

Still working out the arm balancing math...

I'm computing each arm's split based on the relative weights of its two sides, clamping the fraction so neither side gets too short, then deriving the endpoints and child mobile positions from that. I'm also estimating the total part count across all the arms, hooks, and beads to keep the mobile's complexity in check.

Thinking about adding small coil details at the wire joints for a more hand-crafted Calder-like look, possibly pulling a coil helper from the clockwork kit or building the spiral directly.

Still writing coil geometry...

I'll reduce coils to 2.5 turns with adaptive detail to keep triangle counts manageable, and settle on thicker arm rods (6mm) versus thinner hang wires (2.8mm) to match Calder's proportions, then compose the full spec with per-arm yaw values.

Now I'm defining helper functions for shapes and arms, then building out the actual mobile elements—red leaf, black disc, yellow rings disc, crescent—with their sizes, colors, yaw angles, and attachment points.

Balancing the color palette across pieces, I'm settling on red for the leaf and one disc, yellow for the crescent and star, blue for the amoeba, white for the oval dots and ringed disc, and black for the disc and spiral disc. Defining a small red disc element...

Finishing the arm structure, I'm checking the weight balance between branches so the mobile tips correctly, then verifying there's no visual collision between the oval/amoeba decorations and the other hanging elements given their pivot depths and yaw angles.

I'm also tallying up the decal textures used so far—spiral, rings, dots, signature—and considering adding a fifth, maybe a dotted pattern on the red leaf shape for variety.

Working out the leaf geometry now, placing a vertical midrib with short diagonal veins branching off it, positioned relative to the leaf's asymmetrical outline and centered on its centroid so the texture plane aligns properly after rotation.

Mapping out the texture coordinate system...

Defining decoration placement...

For the signature, I'm sketching Calder's mark as a "C" arc paired with a triangle outline to evoke the "A", sized proportionally with the viewBox so strokes scale correctly with the overall size.

Now I'm working out the mobile's vertical layout — computing the lowest hanging ball to set the overall sink offset, then positioning the canopy top and first arm hinge relative to the hook origin so everything hangs naturally below it, and figuring out the wire connection point between the canopy and the first pivot arm.

Writing builder code...

Defining the crescent shape...

Confirming the winding order stays consistent going both directions around the arcs, with the tips tapering to sharp points at scale. Now I'm sketching the prepare function, which generates the outline points, applies rotation, checks the signed area to ensure correct winding (reversing if needed), and computes the centroid to handle shifting the shape into position.

I'm also working out a hook mechanism that scans edges to find where they cross the centroid's x-coordinate, interpolating the y-value and taking the maximum (falling back to the highest point if no crossing is found), then returning the shifted points along with area and offset data, cached via a map keyed on the spec object. Writing layout code...

Writing wire and coil helper functions...

Placing wrap coils at attachment points...

Writing node-building logic...

Mapping out the veins texture for the leaf plane, sizing it against the raw viewBox coordinates so the outline fits, and settling on cream/white tints for the decorative strokes across both faces.

For the signature decal, I'm sizing it relative to its viewBox and deciding it only appears on the front face, aligning it with the amoeba's yaw. I need to make sure textured parts can still show their own colors, fix z-fighting with a small decal offset, and now I'm sketching out a lacquer paint function that takes a base color, seed, and thickness.

Writing lacquer shader logic...

I'm darkening the edges relative to the base and blending lighter grain tones for the body, using a brush gradient along a diagonal axis, then switching between edge and brush color based on how aligned the surface normal is with the thickness direction. For white plates I want the edges to read darker for contrast, and now I'm thinking about adding speckled chips as a next detail.

Now I'm building the canopy mount joint and lathing its profile into a shallow dome shape, but I'm noticing the flat top reads as a floating disc rather than a proper ceiling cap, so I'm considering adding a second ring to give it more visual weight.

I'm also adding a small hook eye as a torus below the mount, wiring it down to the arm pivot, and double-checking the joint hierarchy so the mount remains the true root with every other joint properly parented. Writing arm coordinate code...

Skipping the vertical bow since it breaks the pivot constraint, I'll keep hook-out vectors pointing along the arm direction at each end, with endpoints landing exactly on endA/endB and round caps on the sweeps. I'm also planning two coil wraps per hanging wire, one near the top hook and one at the bottom attach point.

Estimating around 44 total coils at low poly count keeps triangle count manageable, adding roughly 44 parts to reach about 170 overall. For decals, I'm planning plane geometry pieces textured and tinted, aligned to face outward using the bone's direction and up vectors, with a separate texture factory generating a spiral pattern procedurally.

Writing vein path coordinates...
